title: 552. Discrete Mathematics, Counting & Graph Theory: Arrangements with Position Restrictions
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Count arrangements in which one object has a prescribed position.
questions.question: Four runners line up in a row for a photograph, and the team captain must stand at the left end. How many line-ups are possible?
questions.explanation: The captain's place is fixed, and the other three runners can fill the remaining places in \(3!=6\) ways. The number \(24=4!\) counts the line-ups with no restriction.
questions.hint: Once the captain is placed, only three people remain to be arranged.

questions.learningObjective: Count arrangements in which two given objects occupy the ends.
questions.question: Five different books are placed in a row. Two particular books must be at the two ends of the row, in either order. How many arrangements are possible?
questions.explanation: The two particular books can be placed at the ends in \(2\) ways, and the other three books can fill the middle places in \(3!=6\) ways. The total is \(2\cdot 6=12\). The number \(6\) forgets that the two end books can be exchanged.
questions.hint: Place the two end books first, then arrange the rest.

questions.learningObjective: Count line arrangements in which two given people are adjacent.
questions.question: Five people stand in a row. In how many arrangements do two particular people stand next to each other?
questions.explanation: Glue the two people into one block. Then \(4\) objects are arranged in \(4!=24\) ways, and the two people inside the block can be ordered in \(2\) ways, so the count is \(24\cdot 2=48\). The number \(24\) forgets the order inside the block.
questions.hint: Treat the pair as a single object, then remember that the pair can be ordered in two ways.

questions.learningObjective: Count line arrangements in which two groups alternate.
questions.question: Three boys and three girls stand in a row so that boys and girls alternate. How many arrangements are possible?
questions.explanation: The pattern is either boy first or girl first, which gives \(2\) choices. For each pattern the boys can be arranged in their places in \(3!=6\) ways and the girls in theirs in \(3!=6\) ways. The total is \(2\cdot 6\cdot 6=72\). The number \(36\) considers only one of the two patterns.
questions.hint: Decide who stands at the left end, then arrange each group in its own places.

questions.learningObjective: Count arrangements of a word in which the vowels form one block.
questions.question: In how many arrangements of the letters of the word ORANGE do the three vowels O, A, E stand next to one another as one block?
questions.explanation: Treat the three vowels as one block. Together with the consonants R, N, G there are \(4\) objects, arranged in \(4!=24\) ways. Inside the block the vowels can be ordered in \(3!=6\) ways. The total is \(24\cdot 6=144\). The number \(36=3!\cdot 3!\) fixes the position of the vowel block instead of letting it move.
questions.hint: Count the block as one object among the consonants, then order the vowels inside it.

questions.learningObjective: Count arrangements in which a class of objects is confined to certain positions.
questions.question: The digits \(1,2,3,4,5\) are each used once to form a five-digit number. In how many such numbers do the odd digits occupy the first, third, and fifth positions?
questions.explanation: The three odd digits \(1,3,5\) fill the three odd positions in \(3!=6\) ways, and the two even digits \(2,4\) fill the two even positions in \(2!=2\) ways. The total is \(6\cdot 2=12\). The number \(36=3!\cdot 3!\) uses the wrong count for the even digits.
questions.hint: Arrange the odd digits in their places and the even digits in theirs, independently.

questions.learningObjective: Count arrangements in which all objects of one kind are adjacent.
questions.question: Four different mathematics books and three different physics books are placed in a row so that the four mathematics books stand next to one another. How many arrangements are possible?
questions.explanation: Treat the mathematics books as one block. The block and the three physics books are \(4\) objects, arranged in \(4!=24\) ways, and the mathematics books can be ordered inside the block in \(4!=24\) ways. The total is \(24\cdot 24=576\). The number \(144=4!\cdot 3!\) fixes where the block stands instead of letting it take any of its \(4\) possible places among the physics books.
questions.hint: Count the block as one object, then order the books inside the block.

questions.learningObjective: Count arrangements in which one person avoids the end positions.
questions.question: Five people stand in a row. In how many arrangements is a particular person, Dana, not at either end?
questions.explanation: Dana can take any of the \(3\) middle positions, and the other four people can be arranged in the remaining places in \(4!=24\) ways, giving \(3\cdot 24=72\). The number \(48=2\cdot 24\) counts the arrangements in which Dana is at an end.
questions.hint: Count the positions that Dana is allowed to take.

questions.learningObjective: Count arrangements in which objects of one kind are separated.
questions.question: In how many arrangements of the letters of the word PICTURE are no two of the vowels I, U, E next to each other?
questions.explanation: Arrange the four consonants P, C, T, R first: \(4!=24\) ways. They create \(5\) gaps, counting the two ends. The three vowels must go into three different gaps, in order: \(5\cdot 4\cdot 3=60\) ways. The total is \(24\cdot 60=1440\). The number \(240=24\cdot\binom{5}{3}\) chooses the gaps but forgets that the vowels are different letters and can be ordered.
questions.hint: Arrange the consonants first, then place the vowels into the gaps between and around them.

questions.learningObjective: Count permutations in which two elements avoid their own positions.
questions.question: In how many permutations of \(1,2,3,4,5\) is \(1\) not in the first position and \(2\) not in the second position?
questions.explanation: Count the complement. There are \(4!=24\) permutations with \(1\) in the first position and \(24\) with \(2\) in the second position; \(3!=6\) have both. So \(24+24-6=42\) permutations violate at least one condition, and \(120-42=78\) satisfy both. The number \(72=120-48\) subtracts the permutations that violate both conditions twice.
questions.hint: Count the permutations that break at least one of the two conditions, taking care not to subtract any permutation twice.
